Workers try to remain useful and decent inside businesses whose basic arrangements are morally deranged. Saunders's comic language makes euphemism, desperation and managerial logic collide. The collection is frequently brutal, but humour is embedded in the way its narrators think, rather than supplied as occasional relief from a serious story.

works.title: Impostures
works.description: Position 114 in the owner-supplied funniest-books synthesis. Attribution: al-Ḥarīrī. Date: early 12th century; English version 2020. Form: Maqāmāt / linked rogue narratives. A travelling rogue survives by changing voices and turning verbal virtuosity into practical deception. Al-Ḥarīrī's artistry is central to the maqāma tradition, but much of its difficulty resides in language. Cooperson's English recreation makes an unusually revealing comparison possible while also reminding readers that translation can create a different experience of the joke.

works.title: Adventures of Huckleberry Finn
works.description: Position 115 in the owner-supplied funniest-books synthesis. Attribution: Mark Twain. Date: 1884 UK; 1885 US. Form: Comic adventure novel. Huck's literal account exposes the gap between accepted morality and what people actually do. River adventures, confidence tricks and competing kinds of foolishness make the novel persistently comic. Its importance is immense, but uneven pacing, the contentious final section and racial caricature keep it lower here than on a ranking of literary greatness alone.

The humour is darker than the premise might suggest, but its Estonian linguistic and folkloric particularity gives it a strong claim to distinctiveness.

works.title: A Dog's Will
works.description: Position 117 in the owner-supplied funniest-books synthesis. Attribution: Ariano Suassuna. Date: 1955 composition; 1957 premiere. Form: Play / popular religious comedy. Performance sharpens the effect, but the play's language, reversals and relationship between cleverness and mercy are already strong on the page.

Its movement toward violence limits laughter, but the exact observation of patronage, desire and public performance gives the comedy substantial force.

Its inventiveness and influence are exceptional; the deliberately repetitive experiment is also less emotionally involving than the novels above it.
